r0.why: Collision, inspiral via gravitational radiation, and neutron star or black hole outcome above the TOV limit all match [1]-[3].

r1.why: Field trillions of times Earth's in 1-2 ms [4], sGRB visible over hundreds of millions to billions of ly [5], and kilonova as transient isotropic longer-wave radiation from decay of ejected heavy nuclei [8].

r2.why: Extreme neutron flux enables the r-process [6], about half of isotopes heavier than iron [7], and discussed since 1998 but widely accepted after GW170817 in 2017 [9].

r3.why: Date, detectors, NGC 4993, Hydra, 140 Mly [10]; 1.7 s delay, ~2 s burst, light 11 h later [11]; sGRB link [12]; kilonova link [13].

r4.why: GW-based Hubble constant method [17], two earlier methods disagreeing by ~10% [18], and Hubble tension possibly settled by kilonovae as standard candles [19].

r5.why: GW190425 in April 2019 at 99.94% [20], no EM counterpart found [21], XT2 from Chandra at 6.6 Gly in 2019 [25], and magnetar seen for several hours [26].

r6.why: Diverse harmful radiation [27], arrival order [28], extinction within 10 pc or from a directed sGRB hit [31] with directional beam [29], rarer than supernovae with precise aim needed [37], so threat extremely low [38].
